43.title: The king dies
43.carry: grief is the cost of love
43.howItsDone: Hindus retell Dasharatha's death and the story of the hermit's son (known in later tradition as Shravan Kumar) as lessons in love, consequence and caring for parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana, the third, who went unasked. Now three are gone, and in the palace, one old man is left with what he promised.

The charioteer who drove Rama, Sita and Lakshmana to the edge of the kingdom comes back alone. The chariot is empty. Dasharatha asks him to tell everything: what Rama said, how Sita looked, whether they were afraid. At midnight, lying beside Queen Kausalya, the old king tells something he's never told anyone. As a young prince, he was proud of one skill: he could shoot an arrow at a sound, in the dark, and hit what he couldn't see. One night by a river he heard what sounded like an elephant drinking. He shot. And a human voice cried out.
screen: `THE CHARIOT COMES BACK EMPTY.` → `A SECRET AT MIDNIGHT.` → `AN ARROW AT A SOUND.`

segments.voice: It wasn't an elephant. It was a young man, a hermit's son, filling a water pot for his parents, who were old and blind. The arrow killed him. Dasharatha carried the water, and the news, to the parents himself. The grieving father spoke a curse: you too will die grieving for your son. Valmiki never names the young man; later tellings call him Shravan Kumar, and tradition holds him up as a picture of a son who cares for his parents. Decades later, the curse arrives. Dasharatha tells Kausalya the whole story, and before morning he dies: grief for Rama, for the crowning that never happened, for the boy by the river, all at once. The king who kept his word dies of it. He loved his son too much to live without him. The tradition doesn't call that weakness; it holds it up as love. One detail from the very beginning of the Ramayana belongs here. Tradition says the poet Valmiki saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of birds, and heard its mate cry. His grief, in Sanskrit shoka, came out of him as a new kind of verse, a shloka: the first line of poetry, and the beginning of this whole epic. So the Ramayana was born from grief, and its first great death is a father dying of love. Grief is the cost of love. Love someone long enough and, one day, the grief comes with it. The story doesn't try to talk you out of that.

segments.voice: Think of a time doing the right thing cost you something, a friendship, a chance, money, or of a loss that still hurts because you loved. Don't try to make it smaller; let it be as big as it is. If you pray, you can offer that grief to God; if not, let it sit with you, like a guest.

44.title: Bharata refuses the throne
44.hook: the brother who won't take what isn't his; the sandals on the throne
44.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Bharata as the model of selfless brotherhood; the meeting at Chitrakoot and the sandals on the throne are much-loved scenes in Ramlila and in temple art.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shoka, grief, an old curse come due, and a king who died of it. Grief is the cost of love. And the one person all this was for hasn't even heard yet.

Bharata has been away the whole time, at his grandfather's kingdom, far to the west. Messengers tell him only: come home, quickly. He rides for days with a bad feeling. Ayodhya is silent. No music, no crowds. In her rooms, his mother Kaikeyi greets him with the news as if it were a gift. Your father is dead. Rama is in the forest. The kingdom is yours. I did it for you. She's waiting to be thanked. Everything she did, the wishes, the exile, a husband's death, was for this moment.
screen: `BHARATA RIDES HOME.` → `A SILENT CITY.` → `THE KINGDOM IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Bharata doesn't thank her. He's horrified. In Valmiki he turns on his mother with fury and grief: you've destroyed this family, and you've made me the reason. He performs his father's funeral rites, then says what he'll do with the throne. Nothing. It isn't mine. He gathers the mothers, the priests, the ministers and an army, and goes into the forest to bring Rama home. Lakshmana sees the army and assumes the worst: Bharata's come to finish us off. He hasn't. He falls at Rama's feet and begs him to come back and be king. And Rama, who loves him, says no. Our father gave his word; I have to keep it for fourteen years. Two brothers argue, each trying to give the other the kingdom. Neither will take it. So Bharata asks for one thing: Rama's sandals. He carries them back to Ayodhya on his head, sets them on the throne, and rules in Rama's name, a caretaker, not a king. He won't even live in the palace. He moves to a village outside the city, dresses like a hermit, and waits. Fourteen years. Count the voices pushing him the other way: his mother, the law, the empty throne. All of them say it's his. He looks at it and says: not mine. The sandals on that throne are one of the most loved images in the tradition, because they are the opposite of grabbing. For many Hindus, Bharata is the Ramayana's quietest hero.

45.title: The forest years
45.howItsDone: Hindu tradition describes four stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer); today some older Hindus take up a simpler, more devotional life in the spirit of vanaprastha, and Chitrakoot and Panchavati are pilgrimage places.

segments.voice: Yesterday: paduka, Rama's sandals on a throne Bharata wouldn't take. Not mine. Now the three in the forest settle in.

Start with what they left. A prince who grew up with servants and elephants. A princess who wore silk. A brother who rode in chariots beside him. Now: a hut of leaves and branches that Lakshmana built by hand, on a hill called Chitrakoot, beside a river. They wear bark cloth, eat fruit and roots, and bathe in the river at dawn. Rama points out the trees and birds to Sita, the flowers on the hillside, the elephants coming down to drink. For a while, this is the whole story. No battles. No palace. And the strange thing is, in the text, they're happy.
screen: `A HUT OF LEAVES.` → `BARK, FRUIT, A RIVER AT DAWN.` → `THEY'RE HAPPY.`

segments.voice: After Bharata's visit they move deeper south, into the great Dandaka forest, and meet the sages who live in the woods. The sage Atri and his wife Anasuya, a holy woman famous for her devotion, who welcomes Sita like a daughter and gives her gifts and advice. The sage Agastya, who gives Rama divine weapons. The text says they spent about ten years moving from one hermitage to another, learning, listening, living simply. Eventually they settle at Panchavati, by the Godavari river. Today's word: vanaprastha. Vana means forest; vanaprastha is the one who goes to the forest. It's one of the four stages of life in Hindu tradition. First, the student. Second, the householder: work, family, raising children. Third, vanaprastha: when your children have children, you step back from the business of the world and turn toward the inner life. Fourth, the renouncer, who lets go of everything. Traditionally the forest stage comes late. Rama is too young for it; he's there by exile, not by age. But those years look a lot like it. Fewer things. Fewer roles. More attention. When almost everything was taken away, what was left turned out to be enough. One syllable holds it: less.

segments.voice: If you can, put your phone face down or out of reach, and sit with nothing in your hands. Don't plan or fix anything; just notice what's here, your breath, the air on your skin, the sounds around you, like the river at Chitrakoot. For these two minutes you need nothing else; see if that's true.
Vanaprastha. The forest-dweller: the third stage of life, when you step back from the world and turn inward.
Your line: less. A hut of leaves by a river, and they were happy. Day forty-five, done.

46.title: Shurpanakha
46.hook: the demoness's proposal; Lakshmana's cut; the spiral begins
46.howItsDone: Hindus discuss the Shurpanakha episode in many ways: some retellings emphasize the defense of Sita, others, in several Indian languages and in modern writing, tell it with more sympathy for Shurpanakha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vanaprastha, the forest stage, and a hut where less was enough. The peace at Panchavati is about to end, and it ends with a visitor.

A woman walks out of the trees at Panchavati. She's a rakshasi, one of the demon people of the forest, and the sister of Ravana, king of Lanka. Her name is Shurpanakha. She sees Rama and falls for him on the spot, and she doesn't hide it. She walks right up and says: marry me. Leave that woman. I'll be your wife, and we'll roam the forest together. It's bold, and sudden. And the next few minutes set off the war that fills the rest of the Ramayana.
screen: `A VISITOR FROM THE TREES.` → `RAVANA'S SISTER.` → `MARRY ME.`

segments.voice: Rama answers with a joke. I'm married, he says, but my brother isn't. Try him. Lakshmana jokes back: why be the wife of a servant? Go back to my brother. She's sent back and forth until she realizes they're laughing at her. Humiliated and furious, she turns on the one she thinks is in the way, Sita, and rushes at her to kill her. Rama stops her and tells Lakshmana to teach her a lesson. Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears. She runs screaming from the forest, bleeding, to her brother Khara. This is a hard scene, and readers have disagreed about it. Some see Rama and Lakshmana defending Sita from an attack. Others, modern writers among them, are uneasy: the teasing, the cruelty of the punishment, a woman mocked and then maimed. Retellings in different languages handle it differently. Unease here isn't disrespect; it's part of a conversation inside the tradition. Her name means something like the one with nails like winnowing fans, fierce and sharp. Whatever you decide about who was right, look at the chain. A proposal. A joke. A humiliation. An attack. A wound. Next, her brother's army. Then her other brother, Ravana. Then an abduction. Then a war. Each cruelty is a little bigger than the last, and each feels justified to the one doing it. It starts small, often with a laugh. Cruelty compounds.
screen: `A JOKE, SENT BACK AND FORTH.` · `SHE ATTACKS. HE CUTS.` · `READERS STILL DISAGREE.` · `JOKE, WOUND, ARMY, WAR.` · then, large: `CRUELTY COMPOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Think of a small unkind thing, a joke at someone's expense, a cold reply, that grew into something bigger than anyone meant; maybe you did it, maybe it was done to you. Trace the chain, link by link, and ask where it could have stopped: which link could have been a kindness instead?
Shurpanakha. Ravana's sister, whose proposal, mocking and maiming at Panchavati set the whole war in motion.
Your line: cruelty compounds. The chain that began with a laugh isn't finished yet. Until tomorrow.

47.title: Khara's army
47.howItsDone: Hindus who honor Rama as an avatar of Vishnu read his battles as signs of his divine power; many also draw from them the everyday lesson of staying calm under pressure.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha, a joke, a wound, and the spiral beginning. Cruelty compounds. Today, the next link: her brother answers.

Shurpanakha reaches her brother Khara, who rules a garrison of rakshasas in the forest. She falls at his feet, bleeding, and tells him what happened. He sends fourteen warriors to kill the two brothers. Rama brings them all down. So she goes back to Khara, screaming at him for his weakness. This time Khara marches out himself, with his generals and an army. The text gives the number: fourteen thousand. The ground shakes. Dust covers the sun. Against them, in a clearing by a leaf hut: one man with a bow.
screen: `FOURTEEN WARRIORS FALL.` → `KHARA MARCHES OUT.` → `FOURTEEN THOUSAND.` → `ONE MAN WITH A BOW.`

segments.voice: Rama sees bad omens and makes his plan. He tells Lakshmana: take Sita to a cave in the hills, guard her, and don't come out. Lakshmana doesn't argue this time. Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and walks out alone. In Valmiki the sages and the heavenly beings gather in the sky to watch, afraid for him. The battle is enormous: arrows, chariots, a storm of weapons. And the text keeps coming back to one thing. Rama doesn't panic. He doesn't rush. He stands where he is and works. One by one the generals fall, then the army, then Khara himself. When it's over, Sita comes out of the cave and embraces him. This is an epic, and epics tell battles big; you don't have to picture it as a news report. The tradition reads Rama as Vishnu on earth, and it expects the impossible from him. Still, there's something here for people who will never hold a bow. The number didn't decide it. Fourteen thousand is a number designed to make you give up before you start. What decided it was a man who stayed steady, and took the next thing, and then the next. One more detail. One rakshasa escapes the battlefield and runs all the way to Lanka. The spiral isn't finished. Tomorrow, the news reaches the king.

segments.voice: Think of everything coming at you right now, the inbox, the bills, the worries, the to-do list, and let it feel like fourteen thousand. Don't fight it; sit steady, pick the smallest next thing, and hold only that. Everything else can wait for the next arrow.
Khara's army. Fourteen thousand against one; Rama stands steady and wins, and one survivor runs to Lanka.
Your line: steady. Fourteen thousand against him, and one man who didn't rush. That's forty-seven days.

48.title: Ravana hears
48.hook: the ten-headed king; his sister's rage
48.carry: pride listens to the wrong voice
48.howItsDone: At Dussehra many Hindus burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana; many also remember him as a learned devotee of Shiva, and some communities honor him in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khara's army, fourteen thousand against one man who stayed steady. And one survivor ran all the way to Lanka. Today, the king who's been waiting at the end of this story.

Lanka, the golden city. On the throne sits Ravana. Ten heads. Twenty arms. Before you picture a cartoon monster, hear what the tradition says about him. He's brilliant: a great scholar of the Vedas, a master musician, a devoted worshipper of Shiva. Once, the story goes, he tried to lift Shiva's mountain, got his arm pinned under it, and roared so loud that Shiva named him Ravana, the one who roars, or makes the world cry. A king of enormous power and enormous learning. And the messenger from the forest kneels in front of him: Khara is dead. His army is gone. One man did it. His name is Rama.
screen: `TEN HEADS, TWENTY ARMS.` → `SCHOLAR, MUSICIAN, DEVOTEE.` → `THE ONE WHO ROARS.` → `ONE MAN DID IT.`

segments.voice: The messenger adds a suggestion: you can't beat Rama in battle, but he has a wife, Sita, the most beautiful woman in the world. Take her, and he'll die of grief. Ravana likes the idea. He rides to an old rakshasa living as a hermit: Maricha. Years ago, one of Rama's arrows knocked him across the sea. Maricha tells Ravana plainly: don't. Rama is not someone you want as an enemy. Leave this alone. And, remarkably, Ravana listens. He goes home. It could have ended there. Then Shurpanakha walks into his court, disfigured and blazing. In Valmiki she doesn't just ask for revenge; she humiliates him in front of everyone. What kind of king are you, lying around in luxury while men cut up your sister and kill your army? You don't even know what's happening in your own kingdom. Then she describes Sita. That does it. The wise voice said leave it. The furious, flattering, shaming voice said you're weak unless you act. Ravana's pride chose the second. Notice what kind of mistake this is. Ravana isn't stupid. He heard the good advice, and even followed it for a day. But pride has ten heads; it can always find a reason. It hears 'you've been insulted' louder than 'this is a terrible mistake.' The tradition says it cost him everything. Pride listens to the wrong voice.

segments.voice: Think of a time you knew the right thing and did the other thing because someone made you feel small, or of where your pride shows up: needing to win an argument, never asking for help, getting even. Give one of those faces a name and just look at it; the wise voice is easier to hear once you can see the other one.

49.title: The golden deer
49.howItsDone: Hindus often use the golden deer as a picture of maya, the dazzling appearance that misleads; the scene is a favorite in Ramlila, painting and children's retellings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana hears, and his pride chooses the wrong voice. Today he goes back to Maricha, and this time he doesn't ask.

Ravana tells Maricha the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want it. Rama will chase it. While he's gone, I'll take her. Maricha begs him not to; he's felt Rama's arrow once. Ravana gives him a choice: help me and maybe die by Rama's hand, or refuse and die by mine right now. Maricha makes a grim calculation: if I have to die, better it's by Rama. So he goes. One morning at Panchavati, a deer steps out of the trees. It's golden. Its spots shine like silver. Its horns glitter like jewels. There has never been an animal like it.
screen: `BE A GOLDEN DEER.` → `DIE BY RAMA, OR BY ME.` → `A DEER LIKE NO OTHER.`

segments.voice: Sita is picking flowers when she sees it, and she's delighted. Catch it for me, she tells Rama. If you can catch it alive, we'll take it home to Ayodhya when the exile's over. If not, its golden skin would be beautiful. Lakshmana says what's true: there's no such thing as a golden deer. This is Maricha. It's a trick. But Sita wants it, Rama wants to give it to her, and the deer is right there, shining. So Rama picks up his bow, tells Lakshmana to guard Sita and not leave her for anything, and goes after it. The deer leads him deeper into the forest. Close, then gone. Close, then gone. Look at how the trap works. It didn't need force. It needed wanting. Ravana couldn't beat Rama in a fight, so he didn't try; he put something beautiful in the one place it would be seen. Readers sometimes blame Sita for wanting the deer. The tradition is gentler: it's the kind of wanting everyone has, and it catches Rama too, who knew better. That's why the golden deer is one of the tradition's great pictures of maya, your eighteenth word: something that dazzles, and isn't what it seems. Now look back at this week. A king died of love. A brother said not mine. A family lived with less. A joke became a wound. One man stood steady. A proud king chose the wrong voice. And a deer too beautiful to be real walked out of the trees.
